Consult Summary:
- 72-year-old male with established heart failure presents with progressive shortness of breath and new ankle swelling, suggestive of heart failure exacerbation.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Progressive shortness of breath over the past two weeks, worsening in the last few days; new-onset bilateral ankle swelling in the past few days.
- Associated symptoms: Mild, non-troublesome dry cough. No chest pain, palpitations, fevers, or significant lethargy. Appetite and urination unchanged (reports increased urination since starting medication).
- Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, palpitations, fever, or reduced appetite.
- Past medical history: Heart failure (date of diagnosis unspecified); previous “small heart attack” ~5 years ago, required brief hospitalization.
- Medications: Furosemide (dose/frequency not documented; plan to increase), Aspirin (dose/route/frequency not documented), Bisoprolol (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: None reported.
- Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction in early 60s; mother has osteoporosis.
- Social history: Lives alone with two cats; works part-time as a lorry driver (day shifts only). Former smoker (~25 pack-years; quit date not specified). Does not drink alcohol. Light exercise (walks to shops daily).

Examination:
- Doctor mentions having examined chest, saturations, and blood pressure—all were “OK.” (No specific values provided.)

Impression:
- Heart failure exacerbation.

Plan:
- Increase Furosemide to one tablet twice daily (exact dose not documented).
- Order blood tests: full blood count, kidney function.
- Arrange echocardiogram.
- Review in 1 week.
- Advise to call sooner if symptoms worsen (increased breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness).

Quality checks:

●	Missing but clinically expected elements: Medication doses/frequencies/routes not specified; allergy status provided; no documented vital signs; weight/BMI not assessed; no documentation of baseline heart failure investigations; unclear previous ejection fraction.
●	No internal conflicts noted.
●	Transcript is clear; brief conversational disruptions but clinical information well elicited and documented.
